title: Ki Teitzei: the stragglers (Deuteronomy 25:17–19)
hookLine: Amalek attacked the weary at the back of the line

cards: Watch a big group on the move and the line starts to stretch. A school trip, a hike, a crowd leaving a stadium. The fast walkers pull ahead.
The middle keeps pace. And at the back, a gap opens: the kid with the blister, the grandmother who needs to rest, the dad carrying a toddler on his shoulders. Nobody decides to leave them behind.
The line just gets longer. Deuteronomy remembers the day someone noticed that gap and used it.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt; how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were enfeebled in thy rear, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God."
The story itself is in Exodus, a battle at a place called Rephidim, soon after the sea. Deuteronomy adds the detail that matters.

Amalek didn't attack the army at the front. He went for the back of the line: the enfeebled, the faint, the weary, the ones who couldn't fight and couldn't run. He feared not God: no line he wouldn't cross.
The portion ends with a strange double command.
Blot out the memory of Amalek, and, in the same breath: "thou shalt not forget."

teach.h: WHO'S AT THE BACK OF YOUR LINE?
teach.b: Erase the name, keep the lesson.
The rabbis set this passage to be read on the Sabbath before Purim, called Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath of remembering, because tradition traces Haman, the villain of the Purim story, to Amalek.

Some rabbinic authorities hold that the ancient nation of Amalek can no longer be identified, and some teachers read Amalek as a way of acting, preying on the weak, that can show up anywhere, even inside a person.
So the memory has two edges.
Remember what was done to the stragglers. And notice who's at the back of your own line, the one most easily left behind, and most easily hurt.

how: Jews read Deuteronomy 25:17–19 aloud on Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath before Purim, and Jewish law treats hearing it read each year as a duty; it is also read at the close of Ki Teitzei in late summer.

games.q: Israel is strung out on the road, just out of Egypt. Amalek attacks. where in the line does he strike?
o: the front, where the leaders are.
the middle, where the supplies are.
the back, where the weary and weak are.
games.why: he smote the hindmost of thee, all that were enfeebled in thy rear, when thou wast faint and weary.

practice: Picture the lines you're part of: your family, your team at work, your friends, your congregation. Who in one of them is falling behind, the coworker quietly drowning, the cousin no one calls, the friend who stopped showing up?
You don't have to fix their life; just picture walking back down the line and keeping pace with them for a while.

wordCard.voice: Ki Teitzei. When you go out. A portion crowded with commandments, ending with the weary at the back of the line.

orig.note: Hebrew: remember. the first word of Deuteronomy 25:17, and the name of Shabbat Zachor.

carryVoice: Your line: watch the stragglers. A week of trees spared, the nearest town, the mother bird, the railing, wages paid by sunset, the forgotten sheaf, and now the back of the line. Day five hundred eleven, done.
